input: Most people think of sourdough as a difficult bread, but the process is mostly waiting. You mix the dough, let it rest, fold it a few times, and then leave it alone overnight. The starter does the real work, slowly fermenting the flour and giving the bread it's sour flavor. The hardest part is learning to read the dough instead of the clock, since temperature and humidity change everything. Once you get a feel for it, you'll find it alot easier than it looks.

I'll write up the postmortem in Notion tommorow morning.

input: Tomatoes are one of the easiest vegetables to grow at home, as long as they get enough sun. Aim for at least six hours of direct light a day, and water deeply a few times a week rather than a little every day. Shallow watering encourages shallow roots, which makes the plants more sensative to heat. Once the first fruits appear, its a good idea to add a layer of mulch to keep the soil moist.

input: I used to keep my to-do list in my head, which worked fine until it did'nt. Now I write everything down in a plain text file at the start of each day. The list isn't fancy, but it forces me to decide what actually matters before the day gets away from me. The affect has been surprising: I finish more, and I worry less about the things I havent gotten to. Its a small habit, but it's changed how I work.

input: Code review is less about catching bugs than about sharing context. When I review a pull request, I'm mostly trying to understand why the change was made and whether it fits with the rest of the system. Bugs do get caught, of course, but the bigger payoff is that two people now understand the code instead of one. That redundancy pays off the first time someone is on vacation and there feature breaks in production. It's also the cheapest form of mentorship I know of, especially for newer engineers who arent sure what good looks like yet.

Their are still a few optimizations we could make, but I'd rather ship this fix first.

input: I spent some time this afternoon looking into why the search results feel slow on the dashboard. It turns out we're making three separate API calls when the page loads, and the last one waits for the first two to finish before it starts. If we batch them into a single request, we should be able to cut the load time roughly in half. I've sketched out the change in a draft PR, but I'd like a second opinon from someone on the backend team before I procede.

Now I treat bedtime like a meeting I can’t skip.

input: There's a particular kind of quiet that settles over a city early on a Sunday morning. The streets are mostly empty, the cafés are just starting to open, and even the buses seem to move more slowly. I've started taking long walks at that hour, partly for the exercise and partly because it's the only time I can hear myself think.

- Replace the shared map with a syncronized store
- Add a regression test that reproduces the bug under load
- Remove the old retry wrapper, which wasnt doing anything useful

I tested this locally with 500 concurrent sessoins and didnt see a single failure. Their is one follow-up ticket in Jira for the metrics dashboard.

input: Most people think of sourdough as a difficult bread, but the process is mostly waiting. You mix the dough, let it rest, fold it a few times, and then leave it alone overnight. The starter does the real work, slowly fermenting the flour and giving the bread it's sour flavor. The hardest part is learning to read the dough instead of the clock, since temperature and humidity change everything. Once you get a feel for it, you'll find it alot easier than it looks.

The hardest part is learning to read the dough instead of the clock, since temperature and humidity change everything. Once you get a feel for it, you'll find it a lot easier than it looks.

input: This change adds rate limiting to the public search endpoint. Requests are now capped at 100 per minute per API key, and anything over the limit receives a 429 with a Retry-After header. The limiter uses Redis so it works across all of our pods, and the threshold is configurable through an environment variable. I seperated the middleware into its own package to keep the handler code readable. Load testing showed no measurable affect on p99 latency.

input: Heads up: we got paged at 2:14 a.m. for elevated error rates on the checkout service. The root cause was a bad config push that pointed the service at the old Postgres replica. I rolled it back by 2:40, and error rates returned to normal within a few minutes. Their was no data loss, but about 300 orders failed and will need to be retried. I'll write up the postmortem in Notion tommorow morning.

input: Tomatoes are one of the easiest vegetables to grow at home, as long as they get enough sun. Aim for at least six hours of direct light a day, and water deeply a few times a week rather than a little every day. Shallow watering encourages shallow roots, which makes the plants more sensative to heat. Once the first fruits appear, its a good idea to add a layer of mulch to keep the soil moist.

input: I used to keep my to-do list in my head, which worked fine until it did'nt. Now I write everything down in a plain text file at the start of each day. The list isn't fancy, but it forces me to decide what actually matters before the day gets away from me. The affect has been surprising: I finish more, and I worry less about the things I havent gotten to. Its a small habit, but it's changed how I work.

input: Code review is less about catching bugs than about sharing context. When I review a pull request, I'm mostly trying to understand why the change was made and whether it fits with the rest of the system. Bugs do get caught, of course, but the bigger payoff is that two people now understand the code instead of one. That redundancy pays off the first time someone is on vacation and there feature breaks in production. It's also the cheapest form of mentorship I know of, especially for newer engineers who arent sure what good looks like yet.

input: This change adress the memory leak in the image processing worker. The worker was holding onto references to every proccessed file, so memory usage grew untill the pod got OOM-killed. I refactered the loop so each buffer is released after it's upload completes. Memory now stays flat at around 300 MB through out a full run. Their are still a few optimizations we could make, but I'd rather ship this fix first.

input: Hosting a dinner party doesn't have to be stressful. The trick is to pick a menu where most of the work happens before you're guests arrive. A braise or a big pot of soup is perfect, because it gets better as it sits. Make dessert the day before, set the table in the afternoon, and leave yourself atleast half an hour to relax. Noone will remember if the napkins didnt match.

input: I spent some time this afternoon looking into why the search results feel slow on the dashboard. It turns out we're making three separate API calls when the page loads, and the last one waits for the first two to finish before it starts. If we batch them into a single request, we should be able to cut the load time roughly in half. I've sketched out the change in a draft PR, but I'd like a second opinon from someone on the backend team before I procede.
